# The Cyclical Law of Chiseling and Construction · Paleontology Series (Seven)

## The Boring Billion: The Part Where Nothing Happened

### I A Flat Line

First, let us place this stretch of time on a timeline the reader will recognize.

About 2.4 billion years ago, the Great Oxidation Event discussed in Essay Four put substantial amounts of oxygen into the air for the first time. About 700 million years ago, Earth froze over several times in succession, turning into a snowball, with ice reaching all the way to the equator.

The term “Snowball Earth” was proposed in 1992 by Kirschvink at the California Institute of Technology in the United States. He was trying to explain something odd: some jumbled beds of rock left behind by glaciers had actually formed near the equator. Researchers later noticed something else. Directly above the glacial deposits there was often a layer of carbonate rock of a kind formed only in warm seas, as though the climate had abruptly turned itself inside out when the ice age ended. Then, about 540 million years ago, the Cambrian began, and animals suddenly sprouted shells, eyes, and legs.

Between the Great Oxidation and Snowball Earth, from roughly 1.8 billion to 800 million years ago, lies a stretch of time a billion years long. That is more than four times the span from the first dinosaurs to the present. Geologists gave it a nickname: the Boring Billion.

Geologists call all that vast expanse before the Cambrian the Precambrian. It accounts for almost nine-tenths of Earth's history, and it bears on a very large question.

Oxygen had entered the atmosphere more than two billion years ago. Eukaryotic cells, too, had long been around. Yet animals did not arrive until around 600 million years ago. What was life doing through that billion-year interval? Why did Earth not push it onward? This is a crucial stretch of history if we want to understand why animals came so late.

The nickname began with some limestone. In 1995, the US researchers Buick, Des Marais, and Knoll were studying a sequence of limestones more than a billion years old in the Bangemall Basin of northwestern Australia. They were measuring the proportions of heavy and light carbon in the rock. Knoll, one of the three, is among the best-known scholars of Precambrian life. We will meet him again in Essay Fourteen.

Essays One and Four introduced this measuring stick. When organisms take up carbon, they favor the lighter kind. Organic matter buried underground is rich in light carbon, leaving the carbon in seawater relatively heavy. Limestone deposited in the sea records the proportions in the water at the time. Measure the balance of heavy and light carbon in a piece of ancient limestone and you can infer, indirectly, how much organic carbon was being buried: the scale on which the biosphere was fixing carbon and putting it away.

Their results were remarkably flat. The values fluctuated within a very narrow band around the mean, and most samples deviated so little that the difference was negligible. This was no conclusion drawn from a handful of specimens. The longest section ran to 2,500 meters; the most distant sections lay about 250 kilometers apart; and sampling extended from the coast to the outer continental shelf. In their paper, they described the period from about 1.6 billion to one billion years ago as the dullest stretch in Earth's history.

A flat line needs explaining in its own right. In other periods, the carbon-isotope curve jumps up and down like an electrocardiogram. Mass extinctions, ice ages, volcanic eruptions: each leaves a spike. Through this billion years, the curve is almost a straight line.

Later, more and more records began to look flat. Large glacial deposits were almost absent. Banded iron formations, with the alternating red and black layers described in Essay Four, rarely formed either.

The deep ocean remained short of oxygen for a very long time. Recognizable eukaryotic fossils were few in kind and slow to change. Little by little, a nickname became the name of an age.

The phrase “the Boring Billion” is generally credited among researchers to Brasier, the paleontologist at Britain's University of Oxford. Brasier was famous for questioning things. In 2002, he publicly challenged what were then widely accepted as the oldest microfossils on Earth: the filaments in roughly 3.5-billion-year-old chert from Western Australia. He argued that these “bacteria” were really look-alikes produced by minerals, setting off a controversy that lasted for years.

He died in a car crash in 2014. He had used the phrase in a book published in 2012, and people often cite that as evidence that he coined it. Yet the first printed occurrence has not been located in the early papers that can be searched. It may well have circulated by word of mouth at meetings and in discussions before appearing on the page. In an influential review published in 2006, Holland, a geochemist at Harvard University in the United States who was then nearing eighty, described the interval from about 1.85 billion to 850 million years ago as “apparently rather boring.” After that, the framework was cited again and again.

Once it entered a review, people stopped asking, “Was this period boring?” They went straight to, “Why was it boring?” An observation waiting to be tested became a premise waiting to be explained. Today the nickname appears in textbooks, popular-science books, and documentaries. For many people, their first introduction to Earth more than a billion years ago is: “That was the time when nothing happened.”

The same period has other names, each trained on something different. In 2013, some researchers called it the “Barren Billion,” emphasizing the absence of major glaciers.

Tectonic researchers tend to prefer “Earth's middle age.” Their concern is how continents grew. The dates vary, too. The original limestones covered 1.6 billion to one billion years ago; Holland's review used 1.85 billion to 850 million years ago; a definition based on the scarcity of both glacial deposits and carbon-isotope anomalies gives roughly 1.8 billion to 800 million years ago.

This essay asks just one question. If so many records are flat, what, exactly, is flat? Did the world really change so little through that billion years, or can the measuring sticks we use simply not register its changes?

We cannot go back 1.6 billion years and take a sample of seawater. What we can do is find something left behind from that time, with some property related to the quantity we want to know.

Such a thing is called a proxy. We use proxies in everyday life as well. You cannot see inside an engine, so you look at its coolant-temperature gauge. The virtue of a proxy is that you can measure it. Its limit lies in the same fact: what it measures is never the thing itself. **What we see is the shadow that billion years cast through several layers of refraction.**

### II Earth at the Time

Let us first see what Earth looked like then.

The days were shorter. At Xiamaling in Hebei, China, a sequence of black shales about 1.4 billion years old contains extraordinarily regular rhythms, layer upon layer: the beat of Earth's orbit and rotation, preserved in sediment.

In 2018, US researchers used those rhythms to calculate that **a day then lasted only about 18.7 hours**, and the Moon was closer to Earth than it is today. Another study, in 2023, suggested that from roughly two billion to one billion years ago, the slowing of Earth's rotation almost came to a halt. For a long time, a day stayed close to nineteen hours. Even the length of a day was flat during that billion years.

A closer Moon meant bigger tides. The tides were more powerful than today's, and coastal tidal flats were broad and level. As the water rose and fell, it left sets of alternating thick and thin laminae in the mud and sand. By counting them, geologists can also work backward to the number of days in a month at the time.

The land was bare. No plants, no animals, no worms in the soil. Rock lay exposed to wind and rain. Only at the water's edge and in damp places might there have been a thin covering of microbial mat, cracking as it dried in the sun and softening again when rain soaked it.

Without plant roots to hold the earth along riverbanks, most rivers were wide and shallow, splitting into many wandering channels. A single rainstorm could wash away great swathes of sand and gravel. Wind swept the naked land, with nothing to stop the dust it raised. Essay Twelve will show how rivers and soils slowly changed once plants came ashore.

During this interval, the continents first assembled into a supercontinent called Nuna, a name taken from an Inuit expression for “the land surrounding the northern ocean.” It is also called Columbia. It later broke apart, and between about 1.1 billion and 900 million years ago the continents came together again as another supercontinent, Rodinia.

The Sun was about a tenth dimmer than it is today, while the air held far less oxygen. Estimates from different methods vary widely. Taken together, they put atmospheric oxygen at roughly one percent to a few percent of its present level.

For comparison, even the thin air at the summit of Mount Everest has about a third of the oxygen available at sea level. The Sun was dimmer, but Earth did not freeze: the atmosphere contained far more carbon dioxide than it does now, and perhaps more methane as well. It was as though the planet had been tucked under a thick blanket.

The ocean was layered. There was some oxygen at the surface, but it quickly ran out below. Most of the deep sea lacked oxygen and held large amounts of dissolved iron. Along parts of the productive continental shelves lay strips of poisonous water containing hydrogen sulfide.

The floors of the shallow seas belonged to stromatolites. These are the stony lumps introduced in Essay One, built as microbes trap sediment in layer after sticky layer. Some looked like upright pillars, some like overturned bowls, some like clusters of cones.

Northern China preserves some of the finest rock sequences from this interval. From Beijing and Tianjin to the Yanshan Mountains in Hebei, there was once a long bay. Over more than a billion years, several kilometers of limestone, dolostone, and shale accumulated there.

Chinese geologists divide the strata of this interval into the Changcheng, Jixian, and Qingbaikou systems, named after classic sections in North China. At Jixian in Tianjin, a Mesoproterozoic sequence reaches almost ten kilometers in thickness. Pillar-shaped stromatolites can be seen all over its cliffs. The area became a national nature reserve in the 1980s and one of the standard sections for studying the Mesoproterozoic. Stromatolites took an especially rich variety of forms during this time.

Living stromatolites can still be seen today. At Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, Western Australia, the water is so salty it is almost brine. The snails and little creatures that eat microbes cannot survive there, and gray-black stromatolite mounds crowd the shallows like stone mushrooms crouching in the water. Many shallow seas more than a billion years ago probably looked much like this. The difference was that no animals then existed to graze on them. They had no need to retreat into salty refuges.

Ice is almost nowhere to be found, but it is not entirely absent. Compare the record with the later Snowball Earth and the difference becomes clear. Around the Three Gorges of the Yangtze in Hubei, the Nantuo Formation contains tillites more than 600 million years old: a jumble of stones tens to over a hundred meters thick. Blocks large and small sit haphazardly in mud, scraped by glaciers from a continent that then lay at middle latitudes.

No bed of tillite on that scale has been found between 1.8 billion and 800 million years ago. In 2020, researchers at Britain's University of Aberdeen found a curious bed of stones in a sequence of roughly billion-year-old lake deposits in northwestern Scotland.

Five pebbles of local origin, 3.5 to 9 centimeters long, lay scattered along the same bed over a distance of about 250 meters. The mud layers beneath them had been bent down and pierced; those above had built up around them.

Usually only one thing can press stones into soft lake-bottom mud in that way: floating ice. The ice carries stones away from the shore toward the middle of the lake, melts, and drops them into the mud below.

The lake lay at about 35 degrees south, roughly the latitude of Sydney today. Either it was much colder than places at the same latitude now, or it stood at a very high elevation. A lake that once froze is a long way from a major ice age.

These microbes became visible to us only very late. The blank before the Cambrian was precisely what troubled Darwin. Around 1899, Walcott in the United States found millimeter-sized black disks in ancient rocks of the Grand Canyon. They were among the first Precambrian fossils to receive a serious description, but many people did not believe in them.

The turning point came in 1954. In chert from the shore of Lake Superior in Ontario, Canada, the US researchers Tyler and Barghoorn looked through a microscope and saw filamentous and spherical microbes roughly 1.9 billion years old, their forms unmistakably clear. Only then did Precambrian paleontology truly begin.

The main players in the sea were bacteria, especially cyanobacteria. In sunlit surface waters they photosynthesized, releasing what little oxygen there was. On shallow seafloors they wove mat upon mat, slowly piling up stromatolites.

And life? By this time, the seas already contained eukaryotic cells, the kind with a nucleus. All modern animals, plants, and fungi belong to this group.

Essay Five described how they came into being. Most were single-celled. Under the microscope, they appear as tiny spheres covered in patterns, projections, or spines. Paleontologists call them acritarchs, meaning “of uncertain origin.” Even now, no one can say exactly what organisms many of them were.

Shales more than a billion years old around Ruyang in Henan have yielded large acritarchs covered in networks of ridges and projections. Some reach several hundred micrometers across and can be seen with a magnifying glass. A few organisms had also become multicellular. Bangiomorpha and the 1.6-billion-year-old fossils from North China, discussed in Essays Six and Eight, both lived during this interval. Bangiomorpha comes from Somerset Island in the Canadian Arctic and is about a billion years old. Its cells form slender filaments, with some cells set aside specifically for reproduction. As Essay Six explained, it may be among the earliest known organisms to have reproduced sexually.

So what were eukaryotes doing through this billion years? For a long time, the answer was: not much. Their fossils were few in kind and slow to change, and molecular fossils seemed to contain no trace of them either. Section Four will show how that answer was rewritten in 2023.

### III Which Pillars Are Flat?

“Boring” is a table standing on several pillars. Let us examine them one by one.

The first is carbon isotopes, and it is the sturdiest. What does a value close to zero mean? A rough calculation helps. Under the simplest model, it means that of every five portions of carbon entering the ocean, one became organic carbon buried beneath the seafloor, while the rest settled out as limestone. That is much the same proportion as today. After 1995, more continuous rock sequences in two other Australian basins produced similarly low-amplitude records.

In global compilations, the carbon-isotope values of marine carbonates from this interval generally fall within a narrow band close to zero. Compared with the enormous spikes of other periods, traceable from basin to basin, there are no large swings of comparable scale.

The second pillar is oxygen. That it was low is well established. How low is fiercely disputed. Chromium is an element highly sensitive to oxygen. Only when there is enough oxygen in the air does chromium on land become soluble during weathering, allowing rivers to wash it into the sea. Its balance of heavy and light isotopes changes in the process. A study based on chromium isotopes in 2014 suggested that atmospheric oxygen may have been less than one-thousandth of today's level.

The Xiamaling shales are rich in organic matter and are potential source rocks for oil and gas. Petroleum geologists originally studied them to find oil. In 2016, Zhang Shuichang of China's Research Institute of Petroleum Exploration and Development and his colleagues analyzed these shales. They concluded that about 1.4 billion years ago, oxygen in some local seawater was at least sufficient for certain living sponges to breathe. This corresponded to an atmospheric oxygen level of at least around four percent of today's.

The comparison came from an experiment. In 2014, researchers in Denmark kept a common sponge in water from which they progressively removed oxygen. It could still live when the oxygen level was only 0.5 to 4 percent of the present level. **For the same period, readings from different proxies were more than an order of magnitude apart.**

Each proxy responds to different processes. To turn their readings into a single “percentage of present atmospheric oxygen,” every step has to pass through a model. One estimate published in 2021 suggested that the long-term level was no lower than about one percent of today's.

In 2025, researchers even found tiny bubbles of ancient air sealed inside roughly 1.4-billion-year-old salt deposits. The reading indicated more oxygen than the picture of prolonged, extremely low oxygen levels would suggest. A little bubble offers a very clear snapshot. But it is only one snapshot. It cannot tell us whether the level rose and fell before or afterward.

The third pillar is the structure of the ocean. The modern Black Sea provides a comparison: its surface waters contain oxygen, but below a depth of one or two hundred meters the oxygen is gone, and the deep water is full of hydrogen sulfide. The early picture was of the entire Mesoproterozoic ocean rich in hydrogen sulfide, one great poisonous “sulfidic sea.” Later data redrew it.

In 2015, Sperling and colleagues in the United States assembled about 4,700 shale samples spanning nearly two billion years. They found that most deep water during this interval was oxygen-free and iron-rich. Other studies estimated that waters containing hydrogen sulfide formed only a narrow fringe along the continental shelves, covering a few percent of the seafloor or less.

The fourth pillar is iron ore. Much of the iron ore mined around the world today comes from banded iron formations laid down more than two billion years ago. Anshan in China's Liaoning Province and the Hamersley Range in Western Australia are both examples.

Large banded iron formations really were rare during this period. But a scarcity of iron ore does not mean seawater lacked iron. To become an ore deposit, iron has to reach a place where it can be oxidized, precipitated, and then preserved.

A sequence of strata about 1.4 billion years old does contain substantial iron-rich deposits. What this interval lacked was the chance for all the conditions needed to form a large ore body to come together at once.

The fifth pillar is ice. As the previous section noted, records of major glaciers are exceptionally scarce. The dropstones in the Scottish lake show only that ice existed locally.

The sixth is the diversity of eukaryotic fossils. In 2015, Cohen and Macdonald in the United States built a database of Precambrian eukaryotic fossils. Their calculations showed that throughout the Mesoproterozoic, down to about a billion years ago, each fossil assemblage contained relatively few species.

They also offered their own warning. Most samples came from the same ancient continent, and the interval from 1.6 billion to 1.25 billion years ago was particularly poorly studied. In 2024, another study expanded the dataset to 263 stratigraphic sections. The researchers used various methods to correct for age uncertainties and sampling differences, and also performed “rarefaction”: randomly throwing away some of the available samples to see whether the pattern remained.

A pattern that appears only when samples are plentiful will disappear after rarefaction; a real one will persist. Even when the sample was thinned to around two hundred, the picture of persistently low richness from 1.8 billion to 800 million years ago remained.

**The final pillar, as it happens, is not flat at all.** Continents were breaking apart during this interval, too. About 1.27 billion years ago, an enormous magmatic event in northern Canada left hundreds or thousands of parallel dikes underground, fanning out over more than three thousand kilometers. This is the Mackenzie dike swarm, the largest known on Earth. Continents were also colliding and joining together. Rodinia assembled between about 1.1 billion and 900 million years ago. Its name comes from the Russian word for “birth”; later continents are thought to have broken away from it.

The ancient Grenville orogenic belt in eastern North America is the root of a mountain range squeezed up during that assembly. In 2021, a study used an anomaly in one element within zircon to infer that the continental crust had thinned during Earth's middle age and mountains were generally low. It proposed that this “orogenic quiescence” might have left weathering and nutrient supplies inadequate.

That same year, another group of researchers compiled metamorphic and magmatic records and challenged the claim. Mountain building had been widespread and almost continuous across the globe during this interval. What was unusual was the kind of mountains it produced. The crust was very hot. Hot crust is soft and flows sideways readily; it cannot pile up into mountains as thick and high as today's Himalayas. **The plates kept moving. The mountains simply could not grow tall.**

### IV The Invisible Eukaryotic World

In 2023, a study changed how people imagined this billion years.

Brocks of the Australian National University, the geochemist in Essay Five who overturned his own early findings, joined his colleagues in reexamining molecular fossils in rocks more than a billion years old. As Essay Five explained, eukaryotic cell membranes contain a distinctive class of molecules, of which cholesterol is one. They can survive in rock for a very long time, becoming the “fingerprints” of eukaryotic life. Previously, almost none of these fingerprints had been found in rocks older than about 800 million years. The inference was that eukaryotes, even if present, must have been few. The oceans belonged essentially to bacteria.

Brocks's team changed what they were looking for. A modern cell makes cholesterol on a long assembly line. First it produces a long-chain molecule called squalene, originally discovered in shark liver oil. It folds that chain into four connected rings, then trims it step by step: some twenty operations in all. The early stages of the line produce simpler, unfinished molecules.

What if ancient eukaryotes did not yet have such a long assembly line? Perhaps they used those unfinished products in their membranes. The team searched rocks dating from about 1.64 billion to 800 million years ago and found these molecules in large quantities, widely distributed and at high concentrations.

**An invisible eukaryotic world came into view.** The oceans of that billion years may have been full of eukaryotes all along. They used early versions of cholesterol, so the old screening methods had missed them.

The researchers called them the “protosterol biota.” They also found that fingerprints of modern-style cholesterol became abundant only around 800 million years ago. Most of the earlier organisms left no descendants.

**We had found nothing because we were looking for the wrong thing.** Earlier, in 2017, Brocks's team had also found in Australian rocks a sudden surge of algal molecular fingerprints after the first Snowball glaciation, around 650 million years ago. The oceans shifted from bacterial to algal dominance, laying on food for the animals that would follow. These unfinished molecules may also have other sources, including certain bacteria. That possibility is still being tested.

New discoveries have kept coming from fossils as well. In a roughly 1.6-billion-year-old dolostone sequence in central India, filamentous and leaflike fossils preserve cells in three dimensions. In 2017, Bengtson of the Swedish Museum of Natural History and colleagues used synchrotron scans to reveal their orderly cell arrangements. Some cells even contained structures resembling pyrenoids, which help make starch in the chloroplasts of red algae. They suggested that the fossils might be red algae. If so, they would predate Bangiomorpha by more than five hundred million years.

In 2016, Zhu Shixing of the Tianjin Center of the China Geological Survey and colleagues found carbonaceous compressions in the Gaoyuzhuang Formation of the Yanshan region in Hebei, dating to about 1.56 billion years ago. Some were long strips, others shaped like leaves. They reached centimeters, even decimeters, in length: strong evidence that large multicellular organisms already existed. Just what group they belonged to remains unclear.

Fungi may have been there too. In 2019, researchers found branching filaments and little spheres in roughly billion-year-old shales in the Canadian Arctic. Their cell walls contained components of chitin. The researchers proposed that these might be among the earliest known fungi.

In 2020, a branching multicellular green alga was found in rocks about a billion years old near Dalian in Liaoning. Only two millimeters long, it had side branches extending from a slender filament and closely resembled a group of green algae common on coastal rocks today. It may be one of the oldest known green algae. The distant ancestors of all living land plants lie among the green algae.

Single-celled acritarchs also provide clear evidence of eukaryotes. In roughly 1.5-billion-year-old shales in northern Australia, a microfossil called Tappania has projections extending from its cell surface. Those projections branch, and new ones can grow out of old walls. To dismantle and rebuild a cell wall as needed requires a cytoskeleton and a capacity for membrane transport. Only eukaryotic cells have these abilities.

Genes point in the same direction. In 2026, another study worked backward from the genes of today's major eukaryotic lineages to estimate when they parted company. It concluded that eukaryotic lineages had continued branching since the beginning of the Mesoproterozoic, even though the fossil-richness curve appeared to stay low and flat for a very long time.

A family can keep splitting into new households while the style of the nameplate on every door stays the same for centuries. Someone counting nameplates will say that little has changed for ages. Someone tracing the family tree will say that the branching never stopped. Neither is wrong.

So this billion years was not a blank. By around 1.6 billion years ago, there were already several candidates for multicellular eukaryotes, some large enough to see with the naked eye.

By about a billion years ago, there were multicellular red and green algae whose place in the family tree is clear. The intervening six hundred million years has yielded plenty of material. It is the identity of each specimen that remains disputed.

Nutrients in the ocean did not follow a level line either. In 2017, researchers measured nitrogen isotopes from nearshore to offshore along a sequence of rocks about 1.4 billion years old in northern Australia. Nitrogen was relatively plentiful near the coast; the farther out to sea they looked, the less usable nitrogen there was. Within the same basin, organisms close to shore and those offshore faced two different worlds. A single global-average curve would flatten that difference away.

Short-lived oxygenation events have also been recognized, one after another. Studies have reported signals of increased oxygenation or weathering around 1.57 billion, 1.4 billion, and 1.1 billion years ago.

By 2015, two ash beds in the Xiamaling shales had been dated to about 1.392 billion and 1.384 billion years ago, each with an uncertainty of around a million years. In 2024, researchers linked an oxygenation disturbance during this interval to the weathering of fresh rock supplied by large-scale volcanic activity. The size and duration of these events, and whether they happened simultaneously across the globe, are still being debated.

### V What the Flat Curves Say

Return to the chain of reasoning in Section One. Carbon isotopes were flat, so the proportion of organic carbon being buried was constant; therefore productivity was constant; therefore the biosphere changed very little. Every step seems to follow naturally. The trouble is that the other links in the chain can change as well.

In 2021, researchers recalculated using a more complete model of the carbon cycle. They found that even with a carbon-isotope curve staying almost flat over long periods, the proportion of organic carbon buried could vary far more than the simple inference allowed. The isotopic composition of the carbon entering the ocean, the separate weathering of carbonate and organic carbon, carbonate burial, the size of the carbon reservoir: several quantities can change together and cancel one another out at the final link.

It is like looking at a bathroom scale. If the reading has not changed for a month, you cannot conclude that the person has neither eaten nor exercised for a month. They may have eaten a great deal and exercised a great deal, with the two balancing out exactly.

A study published in 2026 offered a particularly neat example. Around 1.57 billion years ago, strontium and lithium isotopes recorded a marked anomaly in weathering on land, while the response in carbon isotopes was quite modest.

Strontium isotopes record where the strontium in seawater came from. Strontium weathered out of old continental rocks tends to be heavier; that supplied by undersea volcanoes tends to be lighter. Their ratio in seawater is like a set of scales weighing the contributions of the two sources. Lithium isotopes, meanwhile, are sensitive to how thoroughly weathering proceeds.

When both needles move, weathering on land has changed. Different elements have different cycles, reservoir sizes, and response times. Carbon has a large reservoir and responds slowly. A weathering event lasting a few million years might leave only a little bump on its curve. **Draw only the carbon curve, and the very same history comes out flatter.**

The later fate of stromatolites is thought-provoking too. In 1971, Awramik in the United States noted a marked decline in their diversity in the late Precambrian, around 700 to 600 million years ago.

He proposed that organisms capable of grazing on microbial mats had appeared and were eating the builders of these stones, mouthful by mouthful. Most living stromatolites today survive only in corners like Shark Bay, where even snails struggle to live.

There is another curve that points in exactly the opposite direction. Between about 1.2 billion and 900 million years ago, stromatolites reached their greatest variety of form in the entire Proterozoic, far exceeding the diversity of eukaryotic fossils during the same interval.

One curve is at a low, the other at a high. They are not measuring the same thing. One counts how many kinds of recognizable eukaryote there are; the other counts how many shapes microbial mats grew into. Both can be true.

For prokaryotic diversity, we do not really have a curve at all. Bacteria and archaea have no hard tissues, and their forms are simple. In little spheres and filaments more than a billion years old, we can at best recognize “microbes” or “something like cyanobacteria.” We cannot match them to living species.

Nitrogen fixation, sulfate reduction, methane production, the cycling of iron: all left traces in the rocks of this interval. We can see where these metabolisms operated and on what scale. We cannot count how many kinds of organism were doing the work. The available data do not support the claim that prokaryotes, too, stagnated for a billion years.

Some kinds of flatness have survived these corrections. Large carbon-isotope anomalies traceable across basins really are absent. Records of major glaciers really are scarce. Large iron-ore deposits really are uncommon. The deep sea remained oxygen-poor and iron-rich, and eukaryotic fossil richness remains persistently low even after rarefaction.

Think of a stock-market index. If it has barely moved in ten years, that does not mean every stock in it has stood still. Some may have multiplied in value; others may have plunged. Add the gains and losses together and they cancel out. A global-average curve can likewise average a mass of local changes, moving in opposite directions, into a straight line.

The first-order, long-term average state really was more stable than in many other ages. Second-order events, on scales of millions to tens of millions of years, and regional differences within the same sea were substantially underestimated in the past.

### VI Resolution

Now we can ask a sharper question. If something major had happened during that interval and lasted a few million years, would we be able to see it?

The problem is not radiometric dating itself. In good sections containing volcanic ash, high-precision dating can already achieve uncertainties of plus or minus half a million to a million years. The two Xiamaling ash beds fall within that range.

As Essay Nine explains, zircon in volcanic ash is a natural clock. But most sedimentary beds contain no volcanic ash. Ash has to fall into quiet water and be covered quickly to survive as a distinct layer. Ash falling on a shoal is usually stirred apart by waves; ash falling on land is usually washed or blown away. The minerals in ordinary mud and sand have been carried in from elsewhere. What we date is the minerals' original age, not the age when that layer settled.

Where ash is absent, the only option is to bracket the rocks between the nearest ash beds above and below. If those two pins are a hundred meters apart, all the intervening layers share the same broad uncertainty.

Strata can also have pages missing. In a rock sequence that looks continuous, deposition may have stopped at a particular surface, or currents may have scoured away part of the record. Hundreds of thousands, even millions, of years can be missing between two adjacent layers. Often the naked eye cannot tell.

Geologists call this a depositional hiatus. The more hiatuses a section contains, the greater the chance that a seemingly steady curve is really several fragments stitched together.

The spacing of samples can mislead as well. In those 1995 limestones, samples were typically taken ten to twenty meters apart. Ten meters is a distance in space. Sedimentation rates change: deep water differs from shallow, quiet intervals from stormy ones. The same ten meters could represent ten thousand years or a million. Without a reliable relationship between age and depth, the number of meters alone cannot tell you the number of years.

Compared with later ages, the biggest difference is often not the instruments but the fossils. The Phanerozoic has many fossils of organisms that existed for only a few hundred thousand years. Find one in a layer of mud, and the age of that mud is pinned down.

The ammonites discussed in Essay Eleven are clocks of this kind. They changed rapidly and ranged widely. Ammonites allow Jurassic strata to be divided into intervals of a few hundred thousand years. The Mesoproterozoic lacks such closely spaced time markers. When a stratigraphic point is correlated around the world, its time window can be far wider than the uncertainty of its laboratory age measurement.

The disparity in age anchors is greater still. In the best-studied Phanerozoic strata, a million years often contains several ash-bed dates or fossil zones by which records can be synchronized.

Many Mesoproterozoic basins have only one or two reliable ages for tens of millions of years. The numbers sound impressive: 4,700 shale samples, over ten thousand carbon-isotope records, 263 sections. They must not be mistaken for more than ten thousand evenly spaced points in time.

Hundreds of samples may cluster in a few basins that are well preserved, easy to reach, and already drilled. Meanwhile, dozens of million-year intervals may be covered by only one or two sections. Sampling density needs to be broken down into at least four quantities: the number of samples, the number of independent sections, the number of independent ancient continents, and the number of independent age anchors per million years.

The last two are what the Mesoproterozoic lacks most, and they are also what determine resolution. Collecting a few more samples may take only a few more days. Finding a new section with reliable age control can take years. How closely a stretch of geological history is studied depends in part on which patch of ground, in which country, happens to preserve it.

These rhythms in the strata come from periodic changes in Earth's orbit. In the early twentieth century, while detained during the First World War, the Serbian engineer Milankovitch used pen and paper to calculate how the eccentricity of Earth's orbit and the tilt and wobble of its axis would periodically alter the sunlight reaching each latitude. Those cycles leave a rhythm in the climate and in layer upon layer of sediment. Geologists use it as another clock.

Good sections really do reveal very fine changes. The centimeter- to meter-scale rhythms in the Xiamaling shales were left by orbital cycles. It was from these very rhythms that the 18.7-hour day in Section Two was read. The information is not necessarily missing. What is scarce is a section with that degree of continuity and independent age calibration.

Carbonate rocks themselves can also be rewritten. Once limestone is buried, groundwater passes through it again and again, soaking it and causing it to recrystallize. Later fluids can quietly alter part of its original carbon-isotope record. Geologists have to examine the samples one by one and select those that have suffered little alteration before trusting them enough to draw a curve.

We can now answer at several levels. A local section with rapid deposition, volcanic ash, and dense sampling will usually offer a chance to detect events on a million-year scale.

A basin with ages only at its upper and lower boundaries may squeeze an event lasting a few million years into an uncertainty window tens of millions of years wide. Several basins may all record an anomaly, yet uncertainties in synchronizing them may make it impossible to prove that they record the same event.

Take an example. Suppose a small ice age lasted two million years around 1.4 billion years ago. Suppose it left only a thin bed of tillite, which happened to fall within an age-uncertainty window tens of millions of years wide. In a global comparison, it might then be treated as simultaneous with a warming event elsewhere in the same window. The two might cancel out, or simply be dismissed as local phenomena. Look through only one sluggish proxy, and the event may leave no visible sign of having happened at all.

### VII An Experiment No One Has Done

There is a very direct way to test this.

Find a stretch of Phanerozoic history that we know was full of short-lived events. Take, for instance, the twenty million years around the extinction of the dinosaurs. That interval contains at least one mass extinction, an episode of extreme warmth about 56 million years ago when global temperatures suddenly rose by five to eight degrees Celsius, and several smaller climatic swings. Each left a clear spike in carbon isotopes.

Artificially reduce the number of sections to the Mesoproterozoic level. Enlarge the age uncertainties to several million years. Lower the sampling rate per million years and the geographical coverage. Then redraw the curve using the same methods. See whether it, too, becomes a flat, very “boring” line.

The methods are ready to hand. Rarefaction, standardization, enlarged error margins: all are there in the literature. The material is ready as well. The Phanerozoic offers a wealth of sections with excellent age control. Yet, in the literature currently searchable, no one appears to have joined the two and carried out the full exercise.

Three bodies of work come closest, but they answer different questions. The 2015 study used randomization to test Precambrian diversity curves and found that small-scale fluctuations were very unstable. It did not use the Phanerozoic as a control.

The 2024 study performed rarefaction within the Precambrian data. Its question was, “If already sparse data are made sparser, will the pattern collapse?” The answer was, broadly, no. That question runs in the opposite direction from ours: “If something we know was not flat is degraded, will it become flat?” The third body of work applies statistical treatments to carbon-isotope records, allowing for uncertainty along the time axis. That, too, stops short of a full degraded-record control.

The experiment has two possible outcomes, and both carry weight. If the degraded Phanerozoic becomes flat as well, a substantial part of the “Boring Billion” may have been made by our measuring sticks.

If the great events still stand out clearly on the degraded curves, then the flatness of the Mesoproterozoic is more likely to be real. Either result would move the debate a long way forward.

It would take stratigraphers, geochemists, and statisticians sitting down together. Other fields have done similar things. Researchers studying climate over the past few hundred thousand years often deliberately “blur” a high-resolution ice-core record to mimic the way seafloor sediments preserve information. They ask how much of an abrupt climatic shift lasting a few centuries would remain if it were recorded in seabed mud. This deliberate worsening of a good record has yet to be used systematically in Precambrian research.

“Lower resolution erases events” is certainly true in stratigraphic statistics. “Lowering resolution to Mesoproterozoic levels is enough to manufacture the entire Boring Billion” has not been directly tested by an experiment of this kind. The 2024 rarefaction tests do at least show that the broad pattern of persistently low eukaryotic fossil richness is quite robust to further cuts in sample size.

**The entire cost of this experiment is someone deciding to do it.** A question that can be settled, methods ready to hand, all the data there. No one has carried out the complete exercise.

If this period really was relatively stable, several explanations for the mechanism stand side by side. Nutrient limitation is the most common. Weak weathering meant that rivers delivered little phosphorus to the sea; in oxygen-poor, iron-rich waters, iron minerals adsorbed phosphorus and carried it away. With little phosphorus, marine productivity stayed low, and so did net oxygen production. Algal blooms in modern lakes show the same mechanism in reverse. Sewage and farmland wash large quantities of phosphorus into lakes, and algae run riot.

Nitrogen may have been constrained as well. In 2002, Anbar and Knoll in the United States proposed an ingenious chain of effects. To fix nitrogen from the air, bacteria use an enzyme containing molybdenum. But oxygen-free seawater containing hydrogen sulfide strips out much of the molybdenum and buries it beneath the seafloor.

With less molybdenum, nitrogen fixation becomes harder. Usable nitrogen declines, and eukaryotic algae cannot flourish. A trace metal may have held an entire biosphere to a slower rhythm.

Tectonics and weathering offer another explanation: low mountains exposed less fresh rock, and weathering was slow. Another turns to the length of the day. In 2021, German and US researchers studied a purple microbial mat in a sinkhole on the bed of Lake Huron in the United States. The water there was low in oxygen and rich in sulfur, much like an ancient shallow sea.

They found that the longer the daylight lasted, the more oxygen the mat released into the water. Each day, the oxygen-producing bacteria had to wait for the sulfur bacteria covering them to move aside before they could get to work. Oxygen also needed time to seep out of the mat. With a short day, darkness arrived before much oxygen had escaped. If the day remained close to nineteen hours for a long time more than a billion years ago, this may have been one reason oxygen was so slow to rise.

The final explanation emphasizes negative feedback. Whenever oxygen increased a little, more iron, sulfur, and volcanic gases consumed it, locking it at a low level.

How the “boring” interval ended provides another clue. Around 800 million years ago, the supercontinent Rodinia began to break apart. New coastlines and shallow seas suddenly multiplied, and vast areas of basalt were raised to the surface and exposed to weathering.

Around 810 million years ago, the carbon-isotope curve took its first large downward plunge in hundreds of millions of years. Because it was first recognized in the Bitter Springs Formation of central Australia, it is called the Bitter Springs anomaly. After that, the curve began leaping about again, and Snowball Earth soon followed. The point where the flat line breaks gives us a comparison for understanding why it stayed flat for so long.

All these explanations are plausible. The difficulty is that they can too easily explain everything: almost any observation can be assigned to some feedback or disturbance. To make them testable, we have to say in advance which feedback operates on which timescale, and what we would fail to see without it. The oxygenation pulses around 1.57 billion and 1.4 billion years ago test the claim of strong feedback. If the feedback really was so strong, how could the system still be pushed out of balance?

### VIII It Is the Curves That Are Flat

A construct, as this series uses the word, ultimately amounts to drawing a line. What falls inside counts; what falls outside does not. The line can be drawn by people, as a set of criteria is, or by nature, as a membrane is.

The constructs in this essay are curves: carbon isotopes, estimates of oxygen levels, the forms of iron, fossil richness, the distribution of tillites, the frequency of iron-ore deposits. What can be measured lies inside the line. What cannot lies outside.

In the earlier essays, most constructs lay on the side of the thing being described: the definition of life, the root of the tree of life, a membrane, the chemistry of a planet, a unit at a higher level. Here the construct falls on the describer's side. “The Boring Billion” is a judgment built jointly from curves, sampling, age models, and the sensitivity of proxies. Of those four, only the first comes directly from that distant time. The other three are our own apparatus.

Once we take it apart, the answer falls into three layers. Some flatness is real and has survived correction: the absence of large carbon-isotope anomalies, the scarcity of major glaciers, the rarity of large iron-ore deposits, a deep ocean that remained oxygen-poor and iron-rich, and persistently low eukaryotic fossil richness.

Some flatness dissolves when we come closer. Redox conditions show spatial differences and pulses against a low background. Plates kept moving even though mountains stayed low. Nitrogen varied sharply across a single ocean basin. Eukaryotes were plentiful; they simply used molecules different from today's. Other flatness has no single meaning. A flat carbon curve cannot be read directly as a biosphere that did not change. **Flatness tells us only that this proxy did not change.**

What a construct cannot contain and cannot eliminate, this series calls the remainder. Here there are two kinds. First, a piece of supporting evidence. Most of the eukaryotes Brocks found, the ones using early cholesterol, had disappeared by 800 million years ago, leaving no descendants alive today. They left molecules in rock but no lineage among the living. They are a vivid example of the kind of absence discussed in Essay Two, except that, this time, they happened to leave a calling card in the stone.

The first kind of remainder is the flat carbon curve itself. It is a real record, well preserved, measured more than ten thousand times. This is simply what it looks like. It does not carry the information we keep asking it for: did the biosphere change or not? This is the kind of absence that Essay Eleven will distinguish more finely. A remnant survives, but it does not preserve the property we want to ask about.

The second kind is more straightforward still. The experiment that would downsample the Phanerozoic to Mesoproterozoic levels has its methods ready and all its data in place. Not a single step requires a new observation. It simply has not been done.

**It is not unknowable. No one has yet gone to look.** Unknowable means that no amount of work can bring an answer. Not yet looked at means that, if someone is willing to do the work, the answer is there.

Before his death, Brasier wrote a book about the “blank before the Cambrian” that had troubled Darwin. It was called Darwin's Lost World. It tells of the clues hidden in that apparently empty history, and of how people gradually learned to read them.

On why animals came so late, two schools take sharply opposing views. One says there was not enough oxygen. Large, moving animals consume a great deal of it, and oxygen did not reach sufficient levels until around the time of Snowball Earth.

The other points to the sponge experiment. Simple animals need very little oxygen. Some seawater more than a billion years ago may already have contained enough. What held animals back was something else: nutrients, ecology, or a genetic toolkit for development that had not yet come together. The records of this billion years are the evidence both sides have to fight over.

This billion years also left things to those that followed. Sexual reproduction in Essay Six, multicellularity in Essay Eight, red and green algae, the cholesterol assembly line inside eukaryotic cells: all began or took their settled form during this “boring” interval. The animals that came later made their entrance standing on its shoulders.

Some prefer to call it “Earth's middle age.” In middle age, one day seems much like the next: the same commute, the same work, much the same numbers on the annual medical report.

But the body keeps changing. The changes are slow, and they do not show up in those few indicators. Earth more than a billion years ago may have been just such a middle-aged person.

At first, the name was only three people's impression of a set of limestones. It expanded into a label for an age, then became an anomaly demanding explanation. Now it is being taken apart again into propositions that can be tested separately. Around 1.4 billion years ago, a day lasted a little over eighteen hours, the seas teemed with eukaryotic cells using early cholesterol, and patches of pillar-like stromatolites covered the shallow seafloor. That world may have been livelier than its nickname suggests.

The criteria are still sifting. The sections are still being sampled anew. On that flat line, people have begun to make out a few points. The lineages have not yet been joined up. It is still dividing.
